ca_old_highway_the.blurb: A small roadside outcrop beside Highway 44 east of Viola, in the Lassen area of northeast California, on the south side of the road. Most of the 17 climbs are boulder problems, eleven of them, running from very easy up to about V4 with a cluster at V3 and V4. Six top-rope lines add variety, from 5.7 up to 5.11. Sun and shade are both available, so you can pick a face to suit the temperature. It is little known and low key, better for a short session than a full day, and some of the cracks are grubby.

ca_indian_palisades_corridor.blurb: A short corridor of rock in the Indian Cove campground area of Joshua Tree National Park, reached by a very brief walk. It holds 17 routes split almost evenly between bolted lines and trad lines, nearly all between 5.6 and 5.9, with a couple at 5.10. The best-known lines are easy sport routes, and the rock offers grippy friction slab climbing of the kind Joshua Tree is known for. Short, well-bolted slabs here make a good first slab lead or a warm-up, though the sun can make some lines hot.

ca_horseshoe_slabs.blurb: A compact slab cliff at the south end of Horseshoe Lake above Mammoth Lakes, at roughly 9,000 feet. The 17 climbs are a mix of top-rope setups, a handful of bolted lines and a few trad pitches, mostly 5.7 and 5.8 with a couple of 5.9s, one 5.10 and one easy line. Expect face and friction climbing about 40 feet tall, where balance and footwork count for more than strength. The cliff faces east, so it gets morning sun. Quieter than many crags and well suited to beginners and families, with lake and pines around.
ca_horseshoe_slabs.parking_note: Drive from Mammoth Lakes along Lake Mary Road all the way to its end and leave the car in the Horseshoe Lake lot.
ca_horseshoe_slabs.approach: From the lot, walk south along the west shore of the lake until the obvious buttress comes into view.

ca_ministry_wall.blurb: A big black wall in Scheelite Canyon, a side canyon off Pine Creek near Bishop in the Eastern Sierra, at around 7,300 feet. By count it is a sport wall, with 16 of its 17 climbs bolted and one trad line. Grades are steep: mostly 5.11 and 5.12, with one 5.10 and a couple of 5.13s. The smooth dark patina rewards precise technique and careful footwork more than raw pump. Multi-pitch trad and a famous offwidth sit at either end of the wall, and it stands right beside the Ecstasy Buttress.

ca_b1_boulder.blurb: One of the best-known blocks at Stoney Point in the Los Angeles basin, and the most popular boulder in the park, with crowds on summer evenings. The 17 problems span a wide range, from a few very easy ones through a solid middle group at V4 and V5 to a handful of hard overhanging classics up to V8 on the west, south and east sides. The sandstone is fragile and easily damaged when damp, and holds slowly shrink with traffic, so skip it after rain. Bring pads.

ca_lost_mule_wall.blurb: A secluded trad wall in the Echo Rock area of central Joshua Tree National Park, tucked into a side drainage away from the busier scene at Echo Cove. All 17 lines are trad, mostly moderate: a handful of 5.6s and 5.8s, a few easier climbs, and one 5.11. Some routes can be top-roped and some link together. The brown rock faces southwest and takes sun for most of the day, which makes it a good cold-weather choice. A lower section sits near the bottom of the drainage, with the main wall farther up and the views opening out as you gain height.

ca_pathway_boulders.blurb: A small bouldering spot in the Housekeeping area of Yosemite Valley, at about 4,000 feet, with boulders lying beside a pathway close to a memorial. It lists 17 problems, and the grades are gentle: most are V0, with a scattering of V1 to V3 and a single V4 at the top end, plus one easier problem. That makes it a handy stop for warming up, working on technique or climbing with newer boulderers. It sits alongside the other Housekeeping boulders, so it pairs easily with a visit to the nearby blocks.

ca_lower_cliffs_upper_tier.blurb: The top level of the Indian Springs cliffs just off I-80 near Cisco Grove, in the Sierra foothills at roughly 5,700 feet. Of its 17 climbs, 13 are trad and four are sport, with the bulk at 5.9 and 5.10, a couple of easier lines and one 5.11. The quality rock stands about 50 to 60 feet, offering friction faces, cracks including a classic finger crack, and mixed lines. Getting there means a class 3 scramble up the lower tier's left edge, and most parties rappel back down.
